papers.title: The usefulness of triploid sib records for selection of diploid candidates in rainbow trout breeding programs for growth, processing traits and hypoxia tolerance
papers.abstract: This study investigates the benefits for rainbow trout selective breeding of using triploid performances rather than diploid ones. Its objectives were to estimate genetic parameters, assess genetic correlations between ploidy levels, and evaluate the gain in selection efficiency using triploid sib testing. The traits analysed were growth, carcass traits, fat content, and acute hypoxia tolerance using pedigree-based and genomic models. Results showed that diploids were heavier and longer than triploids at slaughter age. Triploids exhibited greater tolerance to acute hypoxia in this experiment, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. However, heritability estimates for most traits were similar between ploidy levels when genetic models correctly accounted for triploidy and the unequal maternal and paternal chromosome contributions. Incorrectly treating triploids as diploids substantially overestimated genetic variance and heritability values. Genetic correlations between diploid and triploid performances were high for all traits but varied from 0.60 to 0.98. Correlations were particularly high for carcass yield, fat-related traits and hypoxia tolerance indicating that selection based on diploid performance can efficiently improve these characteristics in triploid offspring. Conversely, correlations for body weight and length were lower, suggesting that evaluating triploid relatives could improve selection accuracy for growth. Overall, the findings support diploid-based selection as an effective strategy for improving triploid production traits, particularly carcass yield and flesh quality. Direct evaluation of triploid relatives may provide additional benefits for growth-related traits. The study highlights the importance of appropriate genetic and genomic models and recommends assessing the economic value of triploid performance testing for each target trait.

papers.title: STING deficiency extends median lifespan and mitigates age-related liver pathology in mice
papers.abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is a major driver of chronic inflammation. While acute STING inhibition can reduce neuroinflammation and tissue damage, its long-term impact on longevity remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that genetic deletion of STING extends median lifespan in mice. This survival benefit is accompanied by a marked resistance to age-related hepatic decline. Our findings demonstrate that targeting STING is a promising therapeutic target to extend healthy lifespan.

papers.title: Comparison of the performance of sporophytes derived from narrow and wide genetic crosses between strains of the cultivated kelp Saccharina latissima
papers.abstract: Seaweed mariculture allows sustainable production of large quantities of biomass for multiple downstream applications but the genotypes cultivated by this industry need to be improved to increase efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is important that the genetic improvement of cultivated strains does not lead to the introduction of foreign genetic material into wild seaweed populations, which are already under threat from global heating. To circumvent this problem, efforts are being made to develop breeding approaches based on the use of locally-resourced genetic material. The aim of this study was to evaluate the potential effectiveness of this 'local' breeding strategy compared to a classical breeding approach based on wide genetic crosses. Analyses of growth rates and cell wall composition of F1 hybrids derived from either intra- or inter-population crosses between Saccharina latissima strains from two localities, southern Brittany, France and the Faroe Islands, did not identify any clear advantage of inter- compared to intra-population crosses. Breeding based on locally-resourced strains would therefore appear to be a valid approach for current strain selection programs. The study also established a large collection of gametophyte strains from multiple sites for future breeding programs and showed that these strains retained the capacity to become fertile after more than ten years in culture.

papers.title: Sample overlap in genome-wide association meta-analysis: practical comparisons across significance thresholds
papers.abstract: Meta-analysis is widely used in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to combine evidence across studies without requiring individual-level data. However, as both the number of studies included in meta-analyses and their sample sizes continue to grow, the same participant may be included in more than one study. Such sample overlap induces dependence across studies and violates the independence assumptions underlying standard meta-analysis methods. HostSeq is a Canadian initiative in which 15 clinical and epidemiological studies were assembled with DNA samples from approximately 10,000 Canadians infected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. We observed duplicate samples across different participating studies. This observation raises an important practical question: what is the impact of sample overlap on association results, and when should such overlap be a concern? Motivated by this real problem, we sought to compare five meta-analysis methods and evaluate their performance against a reference mega-analysis in which the true sample overlap is known. We show that when the degree of sample overlap is relatively small, its impact on association results is minimal, even at the genome-wide significance threshold of = 5*10 -8 . We demonstrate these findings through extensive simulation studies and an application to overlapping cohorts within HostSeq.

papers.title: Leveraging synthetic environmental covariates to explore crop genotype by environment interactions
papers.abstract: Environments are unpredictable. Genotype by environment interactions (GEI) further complicate any assessment of genotype performance or stability across diverse environments posing a challenge for plant breeders. Several approaches exist to address this challenge. However existing approaches present a trade-off between scale and interpretability often acting in a 'black box' manner. Here we extend the Finlay-Wilkinson regression on synthetic environmental covariates of Piepho and Blancon (2023) to dissect GEI at the level of individual developmental windows, resolving which growth stages drive GEI and how genotype stability varies across them. Yield data for 961 genotypes from a barley breeding program, tested across 12 environments, is used as a case study to illustrate how this approach can provide valuable insight into the GEI present. Exploring the dynamic impact of environmental variables across growth stages revealed that environmental factors during early grain fill contributed the most to yield GEI variance. Stability was found to be dynamic across development windows, presenting growth-stage-specific yield stability as a new potential breeding target. This approach yields new, growth-stage-resolved measures of yield stability and a new means of dissecting GEI in complex traits, while also opening a route to environmental clustering based on stage-specific GEI patterns.

papers.title: Hybrid Drosophila genomes rapidly purge minority ancestry but repeatedly retain selected regions
papers.abstract: Hybridization is increasingly recognized as a widespread evolutionary process across animals, plants, and fungi, and plays a key role in driving speciation, shaping genetic diversity, and facilitating adaptation. Initial hybrid genomes are rarely observed empirically, making it challenging to observe in real time how competing forces like purifying selection and adaptive introgression interact to shape post-hybridization genomes. Here, we use replicated experimental hybrid populations between Drosophila simulans and D. sechellia to track directly genome-wide evolutionary dynamics across approximately 45 generations post-hybridization. We show that hybrid populations with primarily D. simulans ancestry rapidly recover wild-type levels of fertility and fecundity, whereas populations carrying predominantly D. sechellia ancestry experience persistent fitness reductions and frequent extinction. Genome-wide ancestry trajectories show pervasive purifying selection against minority-ancestry alleles, leading to rapid regression toward majority ancestry across the genome, with stronger purging on the X chromosome than autosomes. Following the initial purging, neutral minority ancestry stabilized at low frequencies across the genome. In striking contrast, we observe repeated increases in D. sechellia ancestry on chromosome 4 and multiple regions on chromosome 3R within D. simulans-majority populations, providing evidence for adaptive introgression. High-density sequencing revealed that these regions were repeatedly retained across independently evolving populations despite near-complete genome-wide purging. Simulations support a model in which recombination rapidly uncouples beneficial introgressed alleles from linked incompatibility-associated alleles during the initial generations, allowing positive selection to act. Our temporal allele-frequency analyses suggest that hybrid genome stabilization of the introgressed regions is highly repeatable but not identical, yielding parallel outcomes across replicate populations. We establish a tractable experimental framework to directly observe how hybrid genomes reorganize in real time, and demonstrate how purifying selection, positive selection, recombination, and stochastic processes interact to restructure hybrid genomes shortly after admixture.

papers.title: A cold-adapted Cas9 nuclease from the deep ocean
papers.abstract: The abundance of CRISPR systems in bacteria and archaea fuels the search for Cas nucleases that perform where established enzymes fail. Deep Ocean 1 Cas9 (DO1Cas9) is to our knowledge the first Cas9 nuclease characterized from the deep ocean, recovered from a metagenomic sample at 1,500 m depth in the Atlantic Ocean. DO1Cas9 shows cold-adapted structural flexibility, thermal susceptibility, salt-dependent stability, higher specificity than SpCas9 and cleaves double-stranded DNA efficiently under cold conditions where mesophilic SpCas9 retains only residual activity. DO1Cas9 edits genomes in diverse organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, zebrafish, the marine tunicate Oikopleura dioica, and the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. In the marine bacterium Marinomonas mediterranea, DO1Cas9 programmed against an invading phage reduced plaquing efficiency about 10-fold more than SpCas9. These results expand the CRISPR-Cas9 toolbox with a nuclease for cold-chain editing and marine biotechnology.

papers.title: GEMS (GWAS Effect Mechanisms via Sequence-to-Function): Unveiling cell type-specific mechanisms for GWAS variants
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have linked thousands of loci to common diseases, yet for non-coding variants, which constitute the vast majority of the signal, the cell types and states through which individual risk variants act remain largely unknown. Here, we develop GEMS (GWAS Effect Mechanisms via Sequence-to-Function), a framework that trains supervised classifiers on multimodal variant effect predictions (ATAC-seq and RNA-seq) from the sequence-to-function model Borzoi and applies SHAP-based attribution to associate individual GWAS variants with the cell types most relevant to their disease association. Applied to asthma, LDL cholesterol, multiple sclerosis, and type 2 diabetes, GEMS prioritizes known disease-relevant cell types concordant with stratified LD-score regression. At the variant level, GEMS associates a median of 58.7% of fine-mapped variants with at least one cell type via ATAC-seq and 65.9% via RNA-seq, extending cellular annotation beyond the chromatin accessibility peaks in the single-cell atlas used for model training. ATAC-seq variant-cell-type associations are significantly enriched in cis-regulatory elements from independent experimental studies not used in model training, and enrichment persists after excluding variants overlapping training atlas peaks. For multiple sclerosis, hierarchical biclustering of variant--cell-type associations partitions risk variants into immune and CNS modules driven by distinct transcription factor families, recapitulating the immune-mediated and neurodegenerative components of the disease and demonstrating that integrative analysis of sequence-to-function predictions can stratify phenotype-associated variants into mechanistically distinct, cell-type-specific regulatory programs.

papers.title: A high-throughput UAV millimetric imaging pipeline for plant density phenotyping reveals high heritability in wheat-pea sole crops and intercrops.
papers.abstract: Within-field diversification, notably through cereal legume intercropping, is a major lever of the agroecological transition. Breeding cultivars adapted to intercropping requires major changes in breeding practices, owing to strong genotype-by-stand-type interactions and the high spatial heterogeneity of low-input field trials. Part of this heterogeneity stems from variation in plant density, a first yield component that strongly influences resource competition and is critical to monitor in intercrops. Given the many plots in such platforms, high-throughput phenotyping of plant density is essential. Over two seasons, we designed a large field trial involving 200 wheat cultivars observed as sole crop as well as intercropped with two pea tester cultivars, in a pseudo-randomized complete block design. Plant density was manually counted on 40 cultivars, alongwith UAV flights at both high and low altitudes. We propose a method to predict plant density from millimeter-resolution RGB images, using linear regression on log-transformed fractional vegetation cover and additional colorimetric and textural indices. We predict total density of wheat or pea in sole crops, or the combined pea+wheat total density in intercrops with relative RMSE of 19.2% and 27.4% depending on season. Thanks to the pipeline, total plant density was predicted across the entire trial, comprising more than 1,000 microplots (200 varieties); this density showed high heritability (0.75-0.85). We provide guidelines regarding the composition of the training set for such intercrop trials. High-throughput phenotyping approaches such as the one proposed here can be instrumental in mobilizing genetic diversity for agroecology.

papers.title: Phenomic selection enables nursery screening for field performance in maize and pea
papers.abstract: Due to economical constraints, breeding programs eliminate most selection candidates at early stages, before their productivity can be evaluated in field trials. Genomic selection partially overcomes this limitation by enabling early prediction of field performance, but its implementation requires large-scale recurrent genotyping that remains inaccessible for many species and breeding programs. Phenomic selection offers a promising alternative by replacing genotyping with inexpensive high-dimensional phenotyping data. However, previous applications have focused on predicting genotypes already evaluated in field trials. We investigated whether phenomic data acquired by unoccupied aerial vehicles (UAVs) from nursery-grown genotypes can be used to predict their performance in field trials. We validated this nursery-screening approach in maize and pea, two species with contrasting biology and canopy structures, supporting its potential transferability to other species. In the most challenging scenarios, average accuracies for yield-related traits were between 0.36 for maize and 0.40 for pea. Simulations indicated that these accuracies can support substantial nursery culling while limiting the risk of discarding superior genotypes. This proof of concept demonstrates that UAV-based phenomic selection can predict the field performance of nursery-grown genotypes without genotyping the selection candidates.

papers.title: Base Editing as a Therapeutic Strategy for Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease caused by Pathogenic UMOD Variants
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by pathogenic UMOD variants (ADTKD-UMOD) is an untreatable monogenic kidney disease in which misfolded uromodulin is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and exerts a toxic gain-of-function effect. Here we systematically evaluate the full spectrum of base editing strategies targeting the UMOD locus. Base editors corrected a representative missense patient variant, p.Cys170Tyr, with A-to-G conversion efficiencies of up to 83.4%, restoring uromodulin trafficking to the plasmamembrane in cell lines and in human 3D kidney tubuloids. Mutation-agnostic inactivation wasachieved by four routes: premature stop codon introduction, splice-site disruption, allele-specific stop codon introduction and promoter attenuation. Maximum on-target efficienciesranged from 44.1% to 71.9%, providing a strategy set applicable across the UMOD allelicspectrum. Endogenous UMOD expression is rarely recapitulated in human cell models,leaving strategies that act on the endogenous gene difficult to assess in patient cells. Wetherefore established CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) of the endogenous UMOD promoterand confirmed its ability to upregulate UMOD expression in human urine-derived cells. Thisapproach further enabled quantification of endogenous UMOD transcript reduction followingbase editing in HEK293 cells. These results establish base editing as a versatile approachfor ADTKD-UMOD and provide a primary human system for testing interventions targetingendogenous UMOD expression, from nucleic acid-based silencing to small molecules.

papers.title: Analysis of single nucleotide substitution in CYP21A2 gene using Alphagenome
papers.abstract: Context: CYP21A2 encodes steroid 21-hydroxylase, which supplies precursors for adrenal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid synthesis. Interpretation of its variants is complicated by a homologous pseudogene, complex alleles, heterogeneous functional assays and uncertain noncoding effects. We integrated observed variation with a reference-locus saturation analysis to distinguish transcriptional, splicing and protein-level mechanisms. Methods: The NM_000500.9 MANE transcript was reconstructed from GRCh38 genomic sequence and verified against RefSeq and UniProt P08686. ClinVar, gnomAD and UniProt records were retrieved with provenance, and a cutoff-limited PubMed search was reconciled against Entrez. AlphaGenome Atlas scores were obtained for every possible single nucleotide substitution across the 3,230-bp transcript span. Reported non-SNV alleles were analyzed by direct AlphaGenome inference. Adrenal, testis, ovary, placenta, liver and kidney expression predictions were calculated. Results: The results include 483 ClinVar records, 3,208 gnomAD records and 82 UniProt natural-variants. All 9,690 locus-wide substitutions were scored, comprising 6,018 exonic and 3,672 intronic substitutions. The coding set contained 3,201 missense, 1,098 synonymous, 147 stop-gained, nine start-lost, eight stop-lost and one stop-retained substitution. Direct inference was completed for 413 additional reported alleles and four context controls. Established splice defects, including c.293-13C>G and c.738+75C>T, showed appreciable splicing scores without corresponding large reductions in predicted total RNA. Clinical classification groups differed in AVI score distributions. Conclusions: A sequence-verified CYP21A2 catalogue connects clinical annotations, population observations, splicing predictions and measured enzyme function. Complete single-base coverage of the defined CYP21A2 transcript was achievable. Regulatory predictions should guide mechanistic experiments and remain separate from enzyme activity, tissue function and clinical classification.

papers.title: Microscale bulk segregant analysis
papers.abstract: The traits of an organism depend on its genetic background and environment. Bulk segregant analysis (BSA) maps quantitative trait loci (QTL) by measuring parental allele frequencies in pools of genetically recombined progeny (segregants). Conventional BSA requires laborious separate sample handling for each cross and environmental condition. Here, we describe a 96-well liquid format for extreme QTL mapping (X-QTL) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We crossed 40 isolates to a common parent carrying mating-type-specific drug-resistance markers at HO, which enabled us to select diploids and haploid segregants in 1 mL cultures. Each well held one segregant pool, which we then grew in deep wells in four conditions: the standard glucose medium, sodium chloride or caffeine added to the standard medium, or acetate replacing glucose as a carbon source. We barcoded DNA samples from each of 384 wells and sequenced them in one Illumina Nova-seq X run. Sequencing data for 181 segregant pools passed quality control steps and was used to map 1,472 QTL in 35 crosses. We replicated a subset of QTL previously mapped in these growth conditions by conventional X-QTL. The 96-well approach increases the throughput of every step of X-QTL, enabling genetic analysis of many more cross and conditions.

papers.title: Influence of the male germline on B chromosome transmission in D. melanogaster
papers.abstract: Selfish genetic elements that bias their inheritance to the detriment to their host are in an evolutionary arms race with host-derived suppressors that neutralize the spread of these elements. The supernumerary B chromosomes recently found in a mutant Drosophila melanogaster laboratory stock are subject to drive (>50% transmission) when passed through the female germline, but through the male germline they experience the opposite of drive, a phenomenon referred to as drag (<50% transmission). Here we show that males from this mutant stock do not have fertility defects, excluding the possibility that sperm carrying more B chromosomes are inviable. Though we revealed irregularities in the germline stem cell (GSC) niche, we show that other aspects of GSCs activity is normal: there is no delay in their mitoses and the B chromosomes appear to be symmetrically segregated during the GSC divisions, suggesting that the asymmetry of these divisions is not likely the source of B chromosome drag. Together, this work lays the foundation for future studies into the mechanism of paternal B chromosome drag in D. melanogaster, which is poised to significantly advance on our understanding of how various genetic and developmental contexts promote disparate chromosome behavior.

papers.title: Single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome reveals cell type-specific functions and disease mechanisms
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy is a significant source of cellular genetic diversity and can cause disease yet its distribution and functional importance across different human cell types are poorly understood. Here we present scMOCHA (Single-Cell Mitochondrial Omics for Cellular Heteroplasmy Analysis), a scalable computational framework that resolves highconfidence, single-cell resolution mtDNA heteroplasmy directly from standard single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Using this tool to interrogate publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and bone marrow (BM) uncovered the single-cell landscape of mtDNA single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and heteroplasmy across ages in human hematopoietic cell types. PBMCs and BM share many inherited homoplasmic and highly heteroplasmic SNVs, whereas somatic SNVs are tissue- and cell type-specific and distributed across the mtDNA genome, suggesting that they arise largely stochastically. mtDNA replication error is a dominant force shaping homoplasmic variants, while oxidative stress potentially drives a significant portion of heteroplasmic and somatic mutations. Importantly, we discover previously unknown cell type-specific and human disease-associated mtDNA SNVs. By coupling mtDNA genotypes with matched single-cell nuclear transcriptomes and structural modeling, we uncover potential molecular mechanisms by which disease-associated mtDNA SNVs impact cellular processes such as inflammation and contribute to disease. Together, these findings define the single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome and reveal previously unrecognized lineage- and disease-associated patterns of mtDNA variation in the human hematopoietic system.

papers.title: Role of small non-coding RNAs in DSB repair in Arabidopsis thaliana
papers.abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) are highly toxic lesions that must be repaired to avoid major losses of genetic materials or genome rearrangements. A number of highly conserved molecular pathways are involved in DSB repair, each resulting in different repair outcomes for a given DSB. Over the past decade, accumulating evidence has revealed the emergence of an unexpected new actor in DSB repair: RNA. Notably, small RNAs have been observed at DSB-flanking sequences and hypothesized to be involved in their repair. However, these DSB-induced small RNAs (diRNAs) were so far observed in studies using reporter systems, and their natural occurrence as well as their role in DNA repair remains debated. To address this question, we investigated diRNA biogenesis in Arabidopsis thaliana using CRISPR/Cas12a to induce targeted DSBs at three actively transcribed loci and one untranscribed locus. We found that 21-nt diRNAs are generated at transcribed loci, in a Dicer-like 4 (DCL4) dependent manner, but not at the untranscribed locus, indicating that active transcription is required for diRNA production. Remarkably, long-read DNA sequencing analysis shows that these diRNAs do not detectably influence DSB repair via either end-joining or microhomology-mediated end-joining. Furthermore, endogenous diRNAs have a modest effect on homologous recombination-associated repair, as impairment of the diRNA pathway in ago2 mutants resulted in only a slight reduction in RAD51 focus formation following Cas12a-induced DSBs. Together, these findings indicate that diRNAs are not essential for DSB repair itself but may function in the post-transcriptional silencing of damaged genes, likely to prevent aberrant transcription until proper repair is completed.

papers.title: Fine-scale maternal structure and high nuclear connectivity in the French populations of the Geoffroy's Bat (Myotis emarginatus)
papers.abstract: The Geoffroy's bat (Myotis emarginatus) is a sedentary species increasingly threatened by habitat alteration. Here, we assessed genetic diversity and population structure in 760 individuals from 18 French maternity colonies using 34 microsatellite markers and mitochondrial D-loop sequences. Mitochondrial data revealed subtle regional structure, consistent with female philopatry, and a broader phylogeographic split between Western Europe and the Greater Middle East, reflecting historical isolation. In contrast, microsatellites showed high nuclear diversity and minimal population structure across France, with weak isolation by distance and kin clustering, indicating extensive male-mediated gene flow. Moreover, demographic inference suggested population stability, consistent with both marker types. This nuclear homogeneity and demographic stability are strikingly similar to the patterns observed in Rhinolophus ferrumequinum populations sampled at the same colonies, suggesting that reproductive aggregation can maintain connectivity even in sedentary species. Overall, M. emarginatus functions as a largely connected population at the national scale, although localized maternal lineages suggest the presence of functional phylopatric units around key maternity sites that warrant protection. Future genome-wide studies could refine conservation strategies by integrating fine-scale female philopatry with male-mediated connectivity.

papers.title: Dog-human gene network colocalization links synaptic signalling and ubiquitination to compulsive disorders
papers.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is highly polygenic, and the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS), with 53,660 cases and 2,044,417 controls, identified only 30 loci, a small fraction of loci estimated to explain its heritability - too few to resolve biological pathways. Pet dogs develop a compulsive disorder (dogCD) similar to OCD. In a GWAS of dogCD with 2,584 dogs from the community science project Darwin's Ark, each dog locus explains at least 40-fold more phenotypic variance than each human OCD locus, giving power equivalent to the human GWAS with 80-fold fewer individuals. Combining the two GWAS identifies a 165-gene network undetectable in humans at current sample sizes. This network is enriched for genes expressed in neurons, particularly in the amygdala and cortex, and comprises four biological processes: excitatory-inhibitory synaptic transmission, axon guidance and neuron recognition, protein ubiquitination, and adenylyl cyclase-activating G-protein-coupled receptor signaling. Like most complex human traits, dogCD risk is likely driven by regulatory variation: fine-mapped dogCD SNPs are non-coding, and dogCD loci are enriched in candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) in a new dog epigenomic atlas spanning eight brain regions. The cross-species network implicates an inherited risk architecture largely outside current OCD pharmacotherapy, and establishes pet dogs as a model for gene network discovery, particularly for conditions underpowered in human studies.

papers.title: From variants to networks: resolving low SNP overlap in dairy cattle meta-analysis through multi-level functional mapping
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to perform a systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for functional traits in dairy cattle, focusing on calving performance and udder health. We hypothesized that despite the limited replication of individual SNPs across independent studies, functionally related variants would converge on common genes, biological pathways, and genomic regions. Following a systematic literature search and a two-stage filtering process, we extracted data from 20 independent articles covering seven traits: direct and maternal calving ease, direct and maternal stillbirth, clinical mastitis, somatic cell count, and somatic cell score. We first conducted a conventional SNP-level meta-analysis, which demonstrated minimal variant overlap across studies, preventing the detection of significant pooled effects. To resolve this low overlap, we mapped the associated variants to higher organizational levels, including genes, proteins, KEGG and Reactome pathways, and quantitative trait loci (QTL), and combined the statistical evidence using Fishers method. This multi-level functional mapping revealed significant biological convergence. At the gene level, we identified shared genes such as CCDC170 linking maternal calving ease and maternal stillbirth, while DCK, TMPRSS11F, and SLC4A4 were significant for udder health traits. Pathway-level meta-analysis highlighted major functional networks, demonstrating that mastitis-related traits were strongly associated with immune response, signal transduction, and cellular stress pathways, whereas maternal calving traits were dominated by endocrine and calcium signaling. Furthermore, our cross-trait overlap analysis identified 35 shared pathways and 30 shared QTL, reflecting a common biological architecture connecting calving difficulties and mastitis susceptibility. Notably, the innate immune system and signal transduction pathways consistently overlapped across multiple functional traits. In conclusion, conventional SNP-level meta-analysis has limited utility for integrating dairy cattle GWAS due to insufficient cross-study marker overlap. Moving from individual variants toward higher-order functional units effectively reveals reproducible genetic signals and functional convergence. The identified genes, biological pathways, and genomic regions offer valuable insights that can be leveraged as biological priors to improve genomic prediction models for dairy cattle health and reproduction.

papers.title: A comprehensive genetic study of the vaginal microbiota composition of Holstein cows
papers.abstract: The vaginal microbiota is a potentially important component of the bovine reproductive tract and has been associated with fertility, health, and production-related traits in cattle. However, the impact of host genetics on the bovine vaginal microbiota and its genetic correlations with animal performance remain largely unexplored. To investigate this, we performed a comprehensive genetic study of the vaginal microbiota in Holstein cows. Vaginal swabs from 681 lactating cows across 18 herds in Northern France were collected, along with records of fertility, milk production, and health traits. The microbiota samples were sequenced for the 16S rRNA gene, generating count tables of amplicon sequence variants (ASV). We estimated genetic parameters for vaginal microbiota -diversity (Chao1, Shannon, and Simpson indices) and {beta}-diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix), as well as the centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed abundances of taxa present in more than 50% of samples. Across the 173 analyzed taxa, heritability estimates ranged from low to moderate (h2 = 0.09 to 0.38) for five genera, three families, eight orders, three classes, and one phylum. Notably, the order Flavobacteriales exhibited the highest heritability estimate. The study also highlighted genetic correlations between heritable microbiota traits and host phenotypes related to fertility, production, and health. Sequence-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identified biologically relevant signals, including a quantitative trait locus (QTL) for the genus Alloprevotella on chromosome 6, with lead variants located within the NAF1 gene. Additionally, two signals on chromosome 17 for the Bacteroidales order and the Bacteroida class co-localized with IL15. Our findings show that host genetics contributes to variation in specific components of the bovine vaginal microbiota and suggest that microbiome-related traits may warrant further investigation as potential indicators in dairy cattle breeding and management research.

papers.title: ABC transporters support Drosophila intestinal stem and progenitor cells during cytotoxic challenge
papers.abstract: Adult stem cells can survive diverse insults, from ionizing radiation to toxic chemicals. In vertebrates, ABC transporter expression and dye-efflux capacity have been associated with stem-cell protection and multidrug resistance. How compound accumulation differs between adult stem cells and their differentiated daughters within an intact tissue remains poorly understood. Here, we show that adult Drosophila intestinal stem/progenitor cells maintain a distinct low-accumulation state for membrane-permeable compounds and that ABC transporters contribute to this phenotype and to the response to cytotoxic stress. Across nine membrane-permeable probes, stem/progenitor cells accumulated eight at lower levels than differentiated enterocytes. We selected tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM), a membrane-permeable fluorescent probe that showed a strong difference in accumulation between stem/progenitor cells and enterocytes, as a quantitative readout for an RNAi screen of all 56 Drosophila ABC-family genes. The screen identified seven candidate transporters whose depletion increased the stem/progenitor-to-enterocyte TMRM fluorescence ratio. Further characterization of one of them, ABCB7, showed that ABCB7-depleted guts contained fewer mitotic cells during cytotoxic drug exposure. These results implicate ABC transporters in lower compound accumulation in Drosophila intestinal stem/progenitor cells and support a role for ABC transporters in their response to cytotoxic challenge.

papers.title: Spatial isotope tracing maps compartmentalized nutrient use across the adult fruit fly
papers.abstract: Drosophila melanogaster is a powerful model for studying systemic metabolism. Although metabolism is compartmentalized across tissues, prior work in adult Drosophila has mostly measured it in dissected tissues rather than in situ, limiting the spatial information that can be gained. Here, we combine whole-fly mass-spectrometry imaging with stable-isotope tracing and flux modeling to quantify metabolic activities across the adult fruit fly in a spatially resolved manner. Across 68 tracer-fed Oregon-R female flies and 187,709 pixels, we map 81 metabolites onto eight annotated regions, including muscle, fat body, gut, and nervous system. Glucose labeling and fitted relative fluxes indicate higher glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid cycle turnover in thoracic muscle than in abdominal fat body; proline labels the nervous system and eye; glutamine the abdominal reproductive system and gut. Alanine carries glucose-derived carbon through the hemolymph and transfers nitrogen into glutamate. In flies bearing yorkie-driven gut tumors, alanine contribution to malate rises in gut and abdomen, and reducing gut alanine uptake lowers tumor burden. Together, this work establishes a framework for quantitative spatial metabolic analysis, showing compartmentalized nutrient use across the adult fruit fly.

papers.title: Pervasive effect of bottom trawling on benthic biodiversity unravelled by metabarcoding across the Tree of Life
papers.abstract: Bottom trawling is the most widespread human disturbance on the seafloor, known to affect seabed structure and benthic biota. Yet, its impact on benthic communities remains documented mainly for taxa identifiable through morphology, leaving microscopic benthic communities largely overlooked. The Gulf of Lion continental shelf has been trawled for decades by French and Spanish fleets, to the point that encountering untrawled reference areas became elusive. Here, we examined prokaryote, protist and Animalia benthic communities at eight stations, using eDNA metabarcoding of core sediment samples, with five primer-pairs. Benthic communities were cross-referenced with contrasted trawling impacts, integrated across three periods: over one month, three years or ten years preceding the sampling. The community composition was primarily structured by ecological habitats, yet, trawling pressure showed association with prokaryotes and Animalia diversity. Diversity was higher at sites trawled more intensively in the preceding month, whereas long-term trawling was associated with a significant erosion of Animalia alpha diversity. Unexpectedly, communities did not display consistent vertical structure and the relative contributions of trawling and hydrodynamic reworking remain unresolved due to the absence of untrawled sites. Overall, our results show that trawling effects extend to prokaryotic compartments rarely considered in impact assessments, providing a proof of concept for eDNA-based assessment, and underline a pervasive long-term effect on Animalia communities. This study also highlights the importance of the timescale used to quantify fishing pressure and underscores the complexity of impact assessment when monitoring begins too late to establish a clear baseline, particularly when no reference site remains.

papers.title: Large-scale pooled selection enables mapping of modifiers of RNAi gene knockdown effects in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Genetic interactions contribute to phenotypic variation, yet most studies characterize them in a small number of reference backgrounds rather than across natural populations. Studying genetic interactions in Caenorhabditis elegans is facilitated by RNAi by feeding, which enables gene-specific knockdowns across many genetic backgrounds without the need to construct individual mutant lines. However, individually screening hundreds of isolates across many RNAi conditions is laborious. Here, we developed a pooled platform that uses whole-genome sequencing to quantify the fitness of hundreds of genetically distinct C. elegans strains competing in a single flask. We leveraged this platform to evaluate RNAi responses in a pooled population of RNAi-sensitive C. elegans strains and identified two classes of QTL that influence RNAi responses. The first class influences responses to knockdowns of specific genes and is exemplified by a QTL that is specific to knockdown of mig-6. The second class influences general RNAi-response across multiple knockdowns. One QTL in this class localized to the right arm of chromosome III and was detected by both GWA and xQTL mapping, which suggests that a common large-effect variant underlies this QTL. We identified a T96K missense change in the dsRNA receptor SID-2 as the underlying causal variant. The 96K allele resides in the extracellular domain of SID-2 and confers increased RNAi sensitivity relative to the 96T allele. We hypothesize that the 96K allele enables greater uptake of ingested lumenal dsRNA through higher-affinity binding to the dsRNA phosphate backbone. The platform we developed enables systematic mapping of genetic interactions across natural populations at a previously impractical scale.

papers.title: Gene-level evolutionary conservation and human constraint decline at comparable rates across the age of onset of Mendelian disease
papers.abstract: Background Gene-level constraint and conservation scores are widely used to prioritise disease genes and to benchmark genomic language models. Purifying selection acts weakly on phenotypes manifesting after reproduction, so these scores are expected to carry less information about late-onset disease. An onset-dependent gradient has been demonstrated for human allele frequencies but not for the gene-level scores used in practice. Results We built an age-of-onset axis for 2,885 Mendelian diseases from Orphanet and fitted cross-species conservation (241-way phyloP) and human-population constraint (shet) on the same 5,322 gene-disease pairs against matched controls, to test whether one decays faster with onset. Their onset slopes differed by 0.23 logit units (97.5% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.56), equivalent to 0.024 units of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in a design resolving 0.049; the interval excludes constraint losing discriminative power faster than conservation by more than 0.011 AUROC units, widening to 0.033 when somatic associations are dropped. The usual explanation, that early-onset disease genes are developmental, pleiotropic and haploinsufficient by construction, did not account for the contrast; conditioning barely moved it. The answer did, however, depend on the constraint metric: three alternatives yielded larger contrasts excluding zero, though paired comparison could not distinguish the estimates. The metrics also diverged on recessive disease genes, with shet ranked below the gene pool (AUROC 0.487) and loss-of-function depletion above it (0.533), though, against matched controls, both ranked them below (0.457 and 0.450). Evolutionary scores improved a non-evolutionary baseline by 17 to 23%, with no onset gradient. Conclusions Conservation and constraint do not lose their value at measurably different rates as disease onset rises, and with only 283 late-onset Mendelian diseases annotated genome-wide, the question cannot be settled more finely. The gene-class explanation does not account for the contrast. Metrics that rank genes near-identically can still yield opposite onset-stratified answers, so a result reported by one metric carries a sensitivity that its confidence interval does not show. No constraint metric identifies recessive disease genes against matched controls, so a pipeline with recessive disease in scope needs a correction that switching metric does not supply.

papers.title: A frameshift mutation in PRICKLE1 causes skeletal dysplasia in Cheviot sheep
papers.abstract: Skeletal dysplasias can occur in animals, including humans, and are attributed to both environmental and genetic causes. As our understanding of the distinguishing phenotypes of different skeletal dysplasias improves, alongside elucidation of the mechanisms and genetic networks that contribute to skeletal development, identifying and controlling genetic mutations in livestock populations has become increasingly possible, including approaches beyond selective breeding alone. Within Scotland an 'achondroplasia' syndrome that was first described in the South Country Cheviot breed of sheep (OMIA 000004-9940), has continued to occur periodically within the same geographical locations, despite culling of affected lambs over many decades. Affected lambs exhibit rounded heads, short legs, a loss of hooves, abnormal stance and short twisted tails. As the condition has been observed in flocks and as progeny from specific ram and ewe matings, and cases have been co-twinned to normal siblings, this suggests a syndrome caused by a recessive genetic condition rather than environmental factors. Through homozygosity mapping and whole genome sequence analyses, we identified a 10 bp deletion in the open reading frame of the PRICKLE1 gene that encodes prickle planar cell polarity protein 1 and is essential for normal vertebrate embryonic development. We identified additional phenotypes present in affected lambs, including a loss of phalanges, neural tube defects, vertebral and articular chondrocyte defects, hair orientation differences and polycystic kidneys, consistent with a loss of PRICKLE1 function based on comparisons to mouse mutant lines. These findings enabled the development of a simple DNA test for the identified PRICKLE1 mutation that was made commercially available to facilitate the elimination of this genetic disease from sheep flocks.

papers.title: The replication checkpoint couples fork progression to the release of transcribed genes from nuclear pores
papers.abstract: The nuclear envelope contributes to chromatin compartmentalization in eukaryotes by anchoring heterochromatin to the lamina and active transcription sites to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs). During DNA replication, chromatin association with the nuclear envelope is thought to act as a topological barrier to DNA polymerases, potentially exacerbating transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs). While limited evidence suggests that the DNA replication checkpoint kinase Rad53/CHK1 promotes the release of genes from the NPC during replicative stress, the global scale and precise regulation of this process remain unknown. Through a candidate-based screen, we demonstrate that gene release from NPCs is a general feature of the cellular response to replication stress, tightly coordinated with replication fork progression. We show that the checkpoint kinases Mec1/ATR and Rad53/CHK1 are both essential for managing gene association with NPCs, but operate in a distinct, stepwise manner: Mec1/ATR triggers the initial dissociation by promoting the removal of RNAPII from the DNA, while Rad53/CHK1 prevents the premature reassociation of transcribed loci by phosphorylating the nucleoporin Mlp1. Finally, we demonstrate that maintaining this control over genes-NPC association is critical for efficient DNA replication under stress. Collectively, our findings reveal that the DNA replication checkpoint integrates genome duplication with chromosome spatial positioning to maintain genome integrity during replication stress.

papers.title: Ethanol stress induces siRNA-mediated epimutations and phenotypic variability in fission yeast
papers.abstract: Epigenetic information is required for the maintenance of gene expression states through cell division. Some epigenetic information can also persist through generations, raising the possibility that epigenetic differences may arise in populations and contribute to evolutionary processes such as drift and natural selection. Evaluating this requires characterising the properties of such epimutations, so that their rate, stability and genome-wide distribution can be assessed. Recent experiments in many organisms have demonstrated that epimutations occur, but have limited stability relative to DNA sequence mutations. However, the extent to which epimutations contribute to evolution is still unclear, in part because it is not clear whether epimutations respond dynamically to environmental conditions. Here, we use the fission yeast S. pombe, in which evolutionarily relevant epimutations have been observed, but not yet systematically characterised, to test whether a physiologically relevant stress, ethanol exposure, leads to changes in the properties of epimutations. Using laboratory evolution experiments with repeated population bottlenecks to minimise selection, we show that epimutations associated with changes in small interfering (si)RNAs occur at a greater rate in ethanol. Ethanol-induced epimutations are enriched at transposable element loci and correlate with changes in transposon expression. Ethanol exposure also increases gene expression noise genome-wide and variability in growth rate; importantly, both these increases are suppressed in mutants lacking siRNAs. Together, these results demonstrate that stress can alter the generation of heritable epigenetic information, and suggest that siRNAs may have a role in promoting phenotypic variability in response to environmental stress.

papers.title: Niche-dependent epistasis within the cancer genome shapes metastatic fitness
papers.abstract: Epistasis, the genetic interaction between loci, directs non-additive genotype-to-phenotype outcomes. Within a multicellular organism, how the tissue niche (E) shapes gene-by-gene epistasis (GxG) and its phenotypic consequences remains poorly studied. Using tumor lung metastasis as an experimental model, we mapped GxGxE through combinatorial CRISPR perturbation coupled with depletion of defined host myeloid populations in mice. The metastatic niche first selects disseminated tumor cells on GxG epistatic fitness, then drives transcriptome convergence regardless of genotype. Removing anatomically distinct myeloid populations reshaped the metastatic epistasis landscape despite identical tumor genotypes. Gene-by-gene-by-environment epistasis therefore operates at the organismal level, with interaction magnitude and sign set by niche cells. Beyond metastasis, our data suggest that the tissue niche conditions how genetic interactions translate into divergent phenotypes.

papers.title: Contextualizing the polygenic basis of human brain shape
papers.abstract: As the most recently evolved neuroanatomical trait of our species, our globular head shape ('globularity') constitutes a promising point of entry to probe possible associations between brain morphology and cognitive traits that may be distinctive of Homo sapiens. To shed additional light on the underlying biology of globularity and its cognitive consequences, we capitalize on data pairing genetic variation to brain shape differences from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of 34,595 adults of European ancestry, and embed genome-wide associations of globularity within genetic variation underpinning up to 75 brain-related traits. Through extensive hypergeometric tests, we observe significant associations between globularity and white matter traits at the gene level, but stronger associations with cerebellar volume, ventricular size, and the fornix at the genomic variant level. Combining conjunctional false discovery rate (FDR) with genetic correlations, we notice homogeneously concordant relations between globularity and the volume of the brain ventricles, and homogeneously discordant relations with glymphatic function. We also unravel more selective, spatially organized relations between globularity and cerebellar volume, white matter connectivity and sulcal width. Spatial permutation tests reveal that sulcal width associations are systematically distributed along a sensorimotor-association gradient of cortical organization. Additionally, correlations of brain- and lifespan-wise gene expression patterns linked to globularity and the brain ventricles highlight recurrent associations with the pentose phosphate metabolic pathway. Finally, deploying an open repository of genetic variant age estimations and an extensive catalog of single nucleotide changes distinguishing hominins, we uncover a coincidence between the establishment of globularity and the time of emergence of modifications in the cerebrospinal fluid proteome. Overall, we provide a finer-grained genetic architecture for globularity, with novel biological associations to traits across evolutionary and developmental timescales, leading us to draw implications for the early development of cognitive networks but also for liabilities to neurodegeneration late in life.
